## The story in four chapters
:::

::: {.chapter-grid}
::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}
01
:::
:::

### Community becomes possible

#### Creekview · mid-1980s

People with very high physical support needs moved from institutional care into community living, demonstrating that extensive support needs did not necessarily require institutional residence.

[Explore the Creekview evidence →](history/creekview.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}
02
:::
:::

### Greater choice over support

#### Enhanced Consumer Participation Model · around 1990

The surviving record begins to show people receiving home support being trained to act as employers and exercise greater day-to-day choice over support.

[Explore the ECPM evidence →](history/ecpm.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}
03
:::
:::

### Direct funding becomes public policy

#### CSIL · 1994–95

Public funding is provided within a defined program while the person gains greater choice and direction over how day-to-day support is organized. Later official records describe a 1994 pilot and province-wide availability in 1995, while the archive preserves disagreement about the exact 1993, 1994, and 1995 chronology.

[Explore the CSIL pilot evidence →](history/csil-pilot.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::

::: {.chapter-card}
::: {.chapter-card-head}
::: {.chapter-no aria-hidden="true"}
04
:::
:::

### An established and adaptable program

#### Later evolution · 2000s → today

CSIL becomes an established program, with later policy also documenting client support groups and CSIL representatives as ways of exercising employer responsibility.

[Explore later evolution →](history/evolution.qmd){.chapter-link}
:::
:::

::: {.story-caution}
**This is a progression of ideas and arrangements, not evidence that one project formally became the next.**
:::

::: {.eyebrow .eyebrow-light}
What actually changed?
:::

## Public responsibility remained. Day-to-day choice moved closer to the person.
:::

::: {.story-models}
::: {.story-model}
::: {.story-model-label}
Conventional delivery
:::

::: {.story-flow}
1. Public funding
2. Health authority or agency
3. Workers scheduled and managed
4. Person receives support
:::
:::

::: {.story-model .story-model-highlight}
::: {.story-model-label}
CSIL
:::

::: {.story-flow}
1. Public funding
2. Person, representative, or client support group
3. Workers scheduled and managed
4. Support organized around the person
:::
:::
:::

::: {.story-shift-note}
Current rules name three employer forms: the person, a CSIL representative, or a client support group. Those forms are documented in [Later evolution](history/evolution.qmd).
:::

:::
:::

::: {.story-relevance}
::: {.story-section-inner}

::: {.eyebrow}
A model with continuing relevance
:::

## More than three decades of experience with person-directed, publicly funded care

CSIL demonstrates that publicly funded home support can be person-directed rather than provider-managed. The person — and, where necessary, a representative or client support group — can take a greater role in organizing support.

::: {.story-close}
That experience is worth understanding as British Columbia considers how more people can be supported safely at home.
:::
